title: A Noetherian normalization is finite over a complete pair with Nagata closed fibre
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative Noetherian integral domain [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], with fraction field $K$, and $J\subsetneq R$ an ideal. Suppose $R$ is $J$-adically complete [def-weil-pbc-adically-complete-ring] and $R/J$ is Nagata [def-weil-pbc-nagata-ring]. Let $L/K$ be a finite field extension [def-pc-field-extension] and let $T$ be the integral closure of $R$ in $L$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]. If $T$ is a Noetherian ring, then $T$ is a finitely generated $R$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. No normality of $R$, separability of $L/K$, locality of $R$ or completeness of $T$ is assumed.

source.place: Marot (1975), Proposition 2.1, printed p.106: Noetherianity of T implies both conditions (2a) and (2b); Nagata R/J implies universally Japanese by Stacks Tag 0334 (proposition-nagata-universally-japanese). This is the application in Proposition 2.3, printed p.107.

proof.text: The definition of integral closure makes $T$ an integral $R$-algebra. Completeness of $R$ implies $J\subseteq\operatorname{Jac}(R)$, where $\operatorname{Jac}$ is the intersection of maximal ideals. Integrality then gives $JT\subseteq\operatorname{Jac}(T)$. Apply Krull intersection over the Noetherian ring $T$ to the one-generated $T$-module $T$: $\bigcap_{n\ge1}(JT)^n=0$. Since $(JT)^n=J^nT$ by expanding products of ideal generators, $T$ is separated as an $R$-module for the $J$-adic topology. In particular $JT\ne T$, since $T$ contains the nonzero domain $R$.

proof.text:
Put $ ar T=T/JT$ and $r=\sqrt{JT}$. By the surjective-image lemma applied to $T	woheadrightarrow ar T$, the ring $ ar T$ is Noetherian; it is nonzero because $JT
e T$ by Step 1. By the minimal-primes lemma, $ ar T$ has only finitely many minimal prime ideals; let $P_1,\ldots,P_m\subset T$ be their pairwise distinct inverse images, which are prime ideals of $T$ containing $JT$. Every prime $P\supseteq JT$ of $T$ contains some $P_i$: order the primes of $ ar T$ contained in $P/JT$ by reverse inclusion; this set is nonempty, and the intersection of a chain of primes is prime (if $xy$ lies in it while $x
otin q_1$, $y
otin q_2$ for members $q_1,q_2$ of the chain, the smaller of $q_1,q_2$ contains $xy$ but neither $x$ nor $y$), so Zorn's lemma gives a minimal member, which is a minimal prime of $ ar T$ since any smaller prime also lies in $P/JT$. In particular $m>0$: the nonzero ring $ ar T$ has a maximal ideal, which is prime. By the radical lemma in $T$, $r= igcap_{P\supseteq JT}P$ over primes $P$; each $P_i$ is such a prime and each such $P$ contains some $P_i$, so $r= igcap_{i=1}^mP_i$. Since $T$ is Noetherian, its ideal $r$ has finitely many generators.

proof.text: For each $i$ put $p_i=P_i\cap R$. It is prime, since the inverse image of a prime under a ring map is prime (apply the defining product criterion), and contains $J$ since $P_i\supseteq JT$. Thus $p_i/J$ is prime in $R/J$, and $(R/J)/(p_i/J)\cong R/p_i$ by the explicit map sending the class of the class of $a$ to the class of $a$. By the definition of the Nagata hypothesis on $R/J$, the domain $R/p_i$ is Japanese. Apply the prime-quotient normalization lemma to $(R,L,T,P_i)$ to obtain that $T/P_i$ is finite over $R/p_i$. Lifting coefficients along $R\to R/p_i$ shows that the same generators generate it over $R$.

source.place: Marot Proposition 2.1, printed p.106, proof of (2) implies (1); simplified under the assumed Noetherianity of T.

proof.text: The diagonal map $T/r\to\prod_{i=1}^mT/P_i$ is injective: a class in its kernel has a representative in every $P_i$, hence in $r$ by Step 2. The product is a finite $R$-module: for each factor choose the finitely many generators of Step 3 and insert them in that coordinate with zero in all others. These finitely many vectors generate the product by coordinatewise expansion. The Noetherian submodule theorem over $R$ therefore makes $T/r$ finite over $R$.

source.place: Marot Proposition 2.1, printed p.106, proof of (2) implies (1); simplified under the assumed Noetherianity of T.

proof.text: Choose generators $a_1,\ldots,a_s$ of the ideal $r$ in $T$. For every $n\ge1$, the finitely many degree-$n$ monomials in these generators generate $r^n/r^{n+1}$ over $T/r$: expand a product of $n$ elements of $r$, and note that changing its coefficient by an element of $r$ changes the product by an element of $r^{n+1}$. Multiplying those monomials by lifts of the finite $R$-generating family of $T/r$ from Step 4 proves $r^n/r^{n+1}$ finite over $R$. Induct on $n$ to prove $T/r^n$ finite: the base $n=1$ is Step 4; for the step lift generators of $T/r^n$ to $T/r^{n+1}$ and append generators of the kernel $r^n/r^{n+1}$. Subtracting a lifted linear combination leaves an element of that kernel. This explicitly proves generation of $T/r^{n+1}$. The same argument includes $r=0$ with its empty generating family.

source.place: Marot Proposition 2.1, printed p.106, proof of (2) implies (1); simplified under the assumed Noetherianity of T.

proof.text: Apply the finitely-generated radical-power lemma in the ring $T$ with its ideals $r$ and $JT$: Step 2 makes $r$ finitely generated and $r=\sqrt{JT}$. Obtain $t\ge1$ with $r^t\subseteq JT$. Therefore $T/JT$ is a quotient of the finite $R$-module $T/r^t$ of Step 5, and the images of its generators generate $T/JT$. Since $J$ acts by zero on $T/JT$, these same images generate over $R/J$: reduce the coefficients modulo $J$.

source.place: Marot Proposition 2.1, printed p.106, proof of (2) implies (1); simplified under the assumed Noetherianity of T.

proof.text: Apply the finite-over-complete-ring lemma with $A=R$, $I=J$ and the $R$-module $M=T$. Its hypotheses are respectively the given $J$-adic completeness of $R$, the separation $\bigcap_nJ^nT=0$ from Step 1, and finiteness of $T/JT$ over $R/J$ from Step 6. It concludes that $T$ is a finitely generated $R$-module. This lemma packages the completion-and-submodule argument at the end of Marot Proposition 2.1; completeness of $T$ was never assumed.
